paragraphs.source_en: Just then the mistress of Blackie's house began shouting at the top of her voice: “Oh! The salmon on the shelf is gone. What a disaster. That wretched black beast has stolen and eaten it again. What a perfectly hateful cat. Just wait till he comes back. I'll show him what I'll do!” The leisurely, peaceful atmosphere of early spring, shaken so rudely by this disturbance, at once turned that tranquil age of blessed calm into something intolerably vulgar. Blackie wore an insolent expression, as much as to say that if his mistress wished to shout, she might shout to her heart's content. He thrust his square jaw forward, meaning, “You heard that, didn't you?” While I had been talking with Blackie I had not noticed, but now that I looked, sure enough, beneath his feet lay a thin salmon bone worth two sen three rin a slice, muddy and discarded. “You're as capable as ever, I see?” Forgetting our earlier disagreement, I could not help offering him that word of praise. Blackie, however, was not the sort to regain his temper so easily over such a bit of flattery. He said, “What do you mean, capable or not capable! You wretch. I eat only a slice or two of salmon and you talk like that. It's outrageous. Don't go saying things that look down on people! Begging your pardon, but I'm Blackie of the rickshawman's house.” So saying, though he did not actually bare his arm and roll up a sleeve, he vigorously raised his right foreleg all the way up to his shoulder. I said, “I knew from the start that you were Mr. Blackie.” “If you knew that, why say ‘as capable as ever’? What is that supposed to mean?” He kept challenging me relentlessly. Had I been human, he would have seized me by the lapels and shoved me about. Just as I was edging back a little and inwardly feeling quite at a loss, the mistress of Blackie's house cried out again: “Hey, Mr. Nishikawa, I'm calling you, Mr. Nishikawa! I've got business with you. Send me one kin of beef at once, do you hear? One kin of tender beef.” The voice ordering beef from the butcher shattered the quiet of the neighborhood. Blackie stood up, braced all four legs outward, and said with a sneer, “Hmph. Since she only buys beef once a year, damn her, she has to shout about it at the top of her lungs. Showing off to the whole neighborhood over one kin of beef; she is a woman beyond handling!” I had no answer, so I listened in silence. Blackie spoke as if that pound of beef had been ordered for him: “I can't be satisfied with just one kin, but it can't be helped, I'll make do. When she buys it, I'll eat it at once!” I said, “This time it really is a feast. Splendid, splendid!” I said this in the hope of sending him home as quickly as possible. “That's none of your business. Keep your mouth shut! You're annoying!” As he said this, he suddenly kicked back with a hind leg and sent the broken frost from the ground flying all over my face. While I, startled, was shaking the mud and water from my body, Blackie had slipped through the fence and vanished without a trace. Most likely he had gone to spy on Nishikawa's beef.

paragraphs.source_zh: 就在这时，老黑家的女主人大声喊叫起来：“哎呀，柜子上的大马哈鱼不见啦，糟啦，又是给那个黑畜生偷吃啦。真是个让人恨死的猫呀。等它回来，看我怎样收拾它！”初春悠闲平静的气氛，经过这番毫无顾忌的扰动，使得那宁静的“清平圣世”一下子变得俗不可耐。老黑露出一副傲慢的神色，好像是在说主人愿意怎样喊叫，就怎样喊叫，一副悉听尊便的样子。它将那四棱下颏向前伸着，意思是说你都听到了吧。刚才和老黑在交谈的时候我未加注意，现在一看，在它的脚下果然有一块每片价值两分三厘钱的薄薄的大马哈鱼鱼骨头，沾满泥土扔在那里。“你还是那么能干呀？”我忘掉刚才的话不投机，情不自禁地奉上了一句赞语。老黑可不会为这么句奉承话就轻易消气的。他说：“什么能干不能干！你这个东西。俺不过吃了一两片大马哈鱼，你就说这种话，真是岂有此理。别尽说小瞧人的话！对不起，俺可是车夫家的老黑呀。”说着，它虽然没有露臂挽袖，却把右前腿用力举起，一直举到肩头。我说：“我压根儿就知道你是黑君呀。”“既然知道，为什么还说‘还是那么能干？’你这是什么意思？”他一个劲儿向我挑战。如果我是人的话，就要被它揪住前胸推推搡搡了。正在我稍稍向后退让，内心感到为难的时候，又传来老黑家女主人的喊叫声：“喂，西川掌柜的，我喊你呢，西川掌柜的！喊你有事儿呀。马上给我送一斤牛肉来，听见没有？要一斤嫩牛肉呀。”向牛肉铺订牛肉的声音，打破了四邻的宁寂。老黑站立起来，把四条腿向外狠狠地抻了抻，一边嘲笑似的说道：“哼，她一年就买一次牛肉，所以，他妈的，一味大声地吆喝。就靠这一斤牛肉向前邻后舍显示她了不起，真是个难调理的娘儿们！”我无法回答，只好默不作声地听着。老黑仿佛认为这斤牛肉就是给他准备的，说道：“只这么一斤，俺是不会答应的，不过，也只好凑合吧，等她买来，俺马上吃掉它！”我说：“这回可真正是美餐哪，太好啦！”我这样说是想把他尽快打发回去。“你别管闲事，少多嘴！讨人嫌！”他说着突然蹬了一下后腿，把浮在地上的霜花踢了我满脸。我吓了一跳，正在抖落身上的泥水的时候，老黑已窜过篱笆墙，无影无踪了。大概是窥探西川的牛肉去了吧。

paragraphs.source_en: When I returned home, the atmosphere in the parlor was different from usual, filled with the feeling of spring, and even my master's laughter sounded cheerful. Thinking this quite strange, I went in from the veranda where the sliding doors stood open, approached my master's side, and saw that an unfamiliar guest had come. His hair was neatly parted, and he wore a cotton haori with a family crest and Kokura hakama; he had the look of a very serious student. Looking beside the small hand-warmer before my master, I saw a calling card next to a Shunkei-lacquered cigarette case, bearing the words: “Introducing Mr. Ochi Tofu, respectfully, Mizushima Kangetsu.” This told me the guest's name, and also made clear that he was a friend of Kangetsu's. Since I had entered in the middle, I could not at once grasp the course of conversation between host and guest, but it seemed to concern Mr. Meitei, the aesthete whom I introduced last time.
